edges.effect_quant: Behavioral diet-quality interventions often produce modest improvements rather than large shifts. In a systematic review of HEI-based weight-loss trials, improvements were commonly in the 4- to 7-point range, while individual nutrition-education RCTs show that some populations improve HEI or fruit-and-vegetable intake and others change only selected components.
edges.population: adults and families exposed to structured nutrition education or diet-improvement counseling programs
edges.mechanism: Nutrition education can improve diet quality by increasing knowledge, skills, goal clarity, and awareness of healthier substitutions. The effect depends on intensity, repetition, and whether the intervention changes actual food practices rather than only knowledge.
edges.summary: Nutrition education can improve diet quality, but the effects are usually modest and variable. Stronger programs tend to pair education with repeated contact, tailored support, or concrete behavior practice rather than information alone.
edges.caveats: Many education trials differ in outcome scales, target foods, and intervention intensity, which makes pooled interpretation messy. Some programs improve one aspect of diet quality, such as fruit and vegetable intake or HEI, without producing broad durable change across the whole dietary pattern.
